lesson.title: Reusing Yesterday's Valid Message
lesson.summary: A replay attack captures a legitimate transmission and retransmits it later, unmodified, to trick the receiving system into treating that old message as a new, valid one.
lesson.body:
Not every attack requires breaking encryption or forging content. A replay attack works even against a transmission that's fully encrypted and completely unmodified, because it doesn't rely on reading or altering the message at all, only on capturing a legitimate exchange and sending an exact copy of it again later. If a protocol simply checks that a message is authentic and well formed, and has no way to tell authentic and well formed apart from authentic, well formed, and already used once before, then a captured message can be replayed successfully even though the attacker never understood what was inside it.

A useful example is an authentication exchange. Suppose a protocol lets a user log in by sending a message that proves they know a secret, and an attacker manages to capture that exact login message as it crosses the network. If the protocol has no built in way to recognize that message as one it has already accepted once, the attacker can simply resend that same captured message later and be authenticated as the user, without ever learning the user's actual secret. This is why the correctness of a protocol, the specific rules it follows for structuring and validating an exchange, matters just as much as the strength of its underlying cryptography. Encryption alone protects confidentiality, it doesn't automatically protect against a message being legitimately decrypted and accepted a second time.

Well designed protocols close this gap in a few standard ways, and it's worth naming them because they show up repeatedly across networking and security. A nonce, a random or unique value generated fresh for each exchange and never reused, means a replayed message will carry an old nonce the receiver has already seen and can reject. A timestamp lets a receiver reject messages that arrive too long after they were supposedly sent, on the assumption that a replay will show up later than any reasonable network delay would explain. A sequence number lets a receiver track which message number it expects next and reject anything that repeats or arrives out of order. Any protocol handling something sensitive, an authentication step, a financial transaction, a command to a device, needs at least one of these defenses, because without one, being able to observe a single legitimate exchange is enough to repeat it.
